notes.definition: The elements in Group 7 are the halogens. They are non-metals with seven electrons in the outer shell and exist as diatomic molecules (F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂). Going down the group, melting and boiling points increase and reactivity decreases, so a more reactive halogen can displace a less reactive one from a solution of its salt.
explanation: Group 7 contains fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine and astatine. They are called the halogens and are non-metals. Each atom has seven electrons in its outer shell, which is why they have similar chemical properties. The atoms share a pair of electrons to form diatomic molecules: F₂, Cl₂, Br₂ and I₂. At room temperature fluorine is a pale yellow gas, chlorine is a green gas, bromine is a red-brown liquid that gives off orange vapour, and iodine is a grey-black solid that forms a purple vapour when heated. In aqueous solution, chlorine is pale green, bromine is orange and iodine is brown.

Going down the group, the relative molecular mass increases (Cl₂ = 71, Br₂ = 160, I₂ = 254) and so do the melting and boiling points. Chlorine boils at −34 °C, bromine at 59 °C and iodine at 184 °C. This is because larger molecules have stronger forces of attraction between them (intermolecular forces), which need more energy to overcome. This explains the change from gas to liquid to solid going down the group.

Halogens react with metals to form ionic compounds (salts) in which the halogen is present as a halide ion with a 1− charge: chloride Cl⁻, bromide Br⁻ and iodide I⁻. For example, 2Na(s) + Cl₂(g) → 2NaCl(s) and 2Fe(s) + 3Cl₂(g) → 2FeCl₃(s). The halogen atom gains one electron to fill its outer shell. Halogens react with other non-metals to form covalent molecular compounds, in which electrons are shared. For example, hydrogen and chlorine react to form hydrogen chloride: H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g).

Reactivity decreases going down Group 7. When a halogen reacts it gains one electron. Going down the group the atoms have more shells, so the outer shell is further from the nucleus and there is more shielding by inner electrons. The attraction between the nucleus and the electron being gained is therefore weaker, so the atom gains an electron less easily and the halogen is less reactive. This is the opposite trend to Group 1, where reactivity depends on how easily an electron is lost.

A more reactive halogen can displace a less reactive halogen from an aqueous solution of its salt. When chlorine water is added to colourless potassium bromide solution, the solution turns orange because bromine is formed: Cl₂(aq) + 2KBr(aq) → 2KCl(aq) + Br₂(aq). Chlorine also displaces iodine from potassium iodide (the solution turns brown): Cl₂(aq) + 2KI(aq) → 2KCl(aq) + I₂(aq). Bromine displaces iodine: Br₂(aq) + 2KI(aq) → 2KBr(aq) + I₂(aq). Iodine cannot displace chlorine or bromine, so there is no reaction and no colour change.

You can use the trends to predict the properties of astatine, at the bottom of the group. It would have a higher melting and boiling point than iodine, so it would be a solid at room temperature, probably very dark in colour. It would be the least reactive halogen and would not displace any of the other halogens from their salts, while all the other halogens could displace astatine from an astatide.
keyFacts: Group 7 elements are the halogens; their atoms have 7 outer electrons.
Halogens are non-metals that exist as diatomic molecules: F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂.
Room temperature: chlorine green gas, bromine red-brown liquid, iodine grey-black solid.
Going down: relative molecular mass, melting point and boiling point increase.
With metals they form ionic salts containing halide ions with a 1− charge (Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻).
With non-metals they form covalent molecules, for example HCl.
A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halogen from an aqueous solution of its salt.
Down the group the outer shell is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so an electron is gained less easily.

keyTerms.definition: The elements in Group 7 of the periodic table: fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine and astatine.
A molecule made of two atoms joined by a covalent bond, such as Cl₂.
The 1− ion formed when a halogen atom gains one electron, for example Cl⁻ (chloride), Br⁻ (bromide), I⁻ (iodide).
A reaction in which a more reactive element takes the place of a less reactive element in a compound.
The sum of the relative atomic masses of the atoms in a molecule, for example Cl₂ = 71.
An ionic compound formed from a metal and a non-metal, such as sodium chloride.
Reduction is gain of electrons (halogen molecules are reduced to halide ions); oxidation is loss of electrons (halide ions are oxidised in displacement).

equations.name: Displacement (general)
equations.formula: more reactive halogen + metal halide → metal halide + less reactive halogen

workedExamples.title: Predicting and writing a displacement reaction
workedExamples.question: Bromine water is added to potassium iodide solution. Predict whether a reaction happens, describe what you would see and write a balanced symbol equation.
steps: Bromine is above iodine in Group 7, so bromine is more reactive.
Bromine displaces iodine: the colourless solution turns brown.
Products are potassium bromide and iodine.
Equation: Br₂ + KI → KBr + I₂ needs balancing: 2 I atoms on the right, so 2KI, then 2KBr.
Br₂(aq) + 2KI(aq) → 2KBr(aq) + I₂(aq). Check: 2 Br, 2 K, 2 I each side.
workedExamples.answer: Reaction occurs; the solution turns brown. Br₂(aq) + 2KI(aq) → 2KBr(aq) + I₂(aq)

workedExamples.title: Relative molecular mass
workedExamples.question: Calculate the relative molecular mass of bromine, Br₂. (Ar: Br = 80)
steps: Bromine is diatomic, so each molecule has two atoms.

workedExamples.title: Ionic and half equations (Higher)
workedExamples.question: Write the ionic equation and half equations for the reaction of chlorine with potassium iodide solution.
steps: K⁺ ions are unchanged (spectator ions), so remove them: Cl₂(aq) + 2I⁻(aq) → 2Cl⁻(aq) + I₂(aq).

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think halogens get more reactive down the group, like Group 1.
misconceptions.right: In fact halogen reactivity decreases down the group, because halogens react by gaining an electron, which becomes harder as the outer shell gets further from the nucleus.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often write chlorine as Cl in equations.
misconceptions.right: In fact chlorine exists as diatomic molecules, Cl₂, so equations must use Cl₂ and be balanced accordingly.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often confuse chlorine (the element) with chloride (the ion).
misconceptions.right: In fact chlorine is Cl₂, a green gas; chloride is the Cl⁻ ion found in salts such as sodium chloride.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think boiling points increase down Group 7 because the covalent bonds get stronger.
misconceptions.right: In fact boiling involves overcoming the forces between molecules, not breaking covalent bonds; these intermolecular forces get stronger as molecules get larger.

realWorld: Chlorine is used to sterilise drinking water and swimming pools because it kills bacteria.
Iodine solution is used as an antiseptic, and potassium iodide is added to some table salt.
Fluoride compounds are added to toothpaste and some water supplies to help prevent tooth decay.
Sodium chloride, a halogen salt, is used in food and to grit roads in winter.
higherTier: Ionic equations for displacement leave out the spectator metal ions, for example Cl₂(aq) + 2Br⁻(aq) → 2Cl⁻(aq) + Br₂(aq) and Br₂(aq) + 2I⁻(aq) → 2Br⁻(aq) + I₂(aq).
Half equations: the halogen is reduced (gains electrons), Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻; the halide ion is oxidised (loses electrons), 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻.
Halogen displacement reactions are therefore redox reactions: the more reactive halogen is the one that is reduced.
examTips: Always write halogens as diatomic molecules (Cl₂, Br₂, I₂) and balance the equation, for example 2KBr not KBr.
Explain reactivity in Group 7 using 'gaining an electron': further from nucleus, more shielding, weaker attraction, electron gained less easily.
For displacement, describe the colour change you would see (colourless to orange for bromine, colourless to brown for iodine) as well as naming the products.
Explain boiling point trends with forces between molecules, not bonds within molecules.
summary: Halogens are Group 7 non-metals with 7 outer electrons and diatomic molecules.
Melting and boiling points increase down the group as relative molecular mass increases.
Reactivity decreases down the group because an electron is gained less easily.
With metals they form ionic halides (1− ions); with non-metals they form covalent molecules.
A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halogen from a solution of its salt.
Higher: displacement can be shown by ionic and half equations (halogen reduced, halide oxidised).

questions.question: How many electrons are in the outer shell of a halogen atom?
markScheme: 1 mark: 7
questions.explanation: Halogens are in Group 7, so they have 7 outer electrons. 17 is the atomic number of chlorine.

questions.question: How do the halogens exist as elements?
markScheme: 1 mark: diatomic molecules
questions.explanation: Halogen atoms share a pair of electrons to form molecules such as Cl₂. Single atoms are typical of the noble gases.

questions.question: How does reactivity change going down Group 7?
markScheme: 1 mark: it decreases
questions.explanation: Fluorine is the most reactive halogen; reactivity decreases down the group, the opposite of Group 1.

questions.question: Which describes bromine at room temperature?
markScheme: 1 mark: red-brown liquid
questions.explanation: Bromine is a liquid. Chlorine is a green gas, iodine a grey-black solid and fluorine a pale yellow gas.

questions.question: Why do the boiling points of the halogens increase down the group?
options: The molecules get larger, so the forces between molecules get stronger
The covalent bond inside each molecule gets stronger
The atoms gain more outer electrons
markScheme: 1 mark: larger molecules, stronger intermolecular forces
questions.explanation: Boiling separates molecules from each other; the bonds inside them do not break. All halogens have 7 outer electrons.

questions.question: Which pair of substances will react together?
options: Iodine solution and potassium chloride solution
Bromine water and potassium chloride solution
Iodine solution and potassium bromide solution
Chlorine water and potassium iodide solution
markScheme: 1 mark: chlorine water and potassium iodide solution
questions.explanation: Only a more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one. Chlorine is more reactive than iodine; in the other pairs the halogen is less reactive.

questions.question: Chlorine water is added to colourless potassium bromide solution. What colour does the solution become?
markScheme: 1 mark: orange
questions.explanation: Chlorine displaces bromine, which is orange in solution. Purple is the colour of iodine vapour.

questions.question: What type of compound is formed when chlorine reacts with hydrogen?
markScheme: 1 mark: covalent molecule
questions.explanation: Hydrogen and chlorine are both non-metals, so they share electrons to form HCl molecules.

questions.question: What is the charge on a halide ion such as bromide?
markScheme: 1 mark: 1−
questions.explanation: A halogen atom gains one electron to fill its outer shell, giving a 1− charge.

questions.question: Why is fluorine more reactive than chlorine?
options: Fluorine's outer shell is closer to the nucleus with less shielding, so an electron is gained more easily
Fluorine loses its outer electrons more easily
markScheme: 1 mark: outer shell closer to nucleus / less shielding / electron gained more easily
questions.explanation: Both have 7 outer electrons. Halogens react by gaining electrons, and the stronger attraction in the smaller fluorine atom makes this easier.

questions.question: Astatine is below iodine in Group 7. Which prediction is most likely to be correct?
options: Astatine is a gas at room temperature
Astatine will displace iodine from potassium iodide solution
Astatine is more reactive than chlorine
Astatine is a solid that is less reactive than iodine
markScheme: 1 mark: solid, less reactive than iodine
questions.explanation: Melting and boiling points increase and reactivity decreases down the group, so astatine is a solid and cannot displace iodine.

questions.question: Which is the ionic equation for the reaction between chlorine and potassium iodide solution?
markScheme: 1 mark: Cl₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + I₂
questions.explanation: The K⁺ ions are spectator ions and are left out. Halogens are diatomic, and the last option is the reverse reaction, which does not happen.

questions.question: In the reaction Br₂(aq) + 2I⁻(aq) → 2Br⁻(aq) + I₂(aq), which species is oxidised?
markScheme: 1 mark: I⁻
questions.explanation: Iodide ions lose electrons (2I⁻ → I₂ + 2e⁻), and loss of electrons is oxidation. Bromine gains electrons, so it is reduced.

questions.question: Calculate the relative molecular mass (Mr) of chlorine, Cl₂. (Ar: Cl = 35.5)
markScheme: 1 mark: 71
questions.explanation: Chlorine is diatomic: 2 × 35.5 = 71.

questions.question: How many electrons are in a chloride ion, Cl⁻? (Chlorine has an atomic number of 17.)
markScheme: 1 mark: 18
questions.explanation: A chlorine atom has 17 electrons and gains one to form Cl⁻, giving 18 (2,8,8).

questions.question: Calculate the relative molecular mass (Mr) of iodine, I₂. (Ar: I = 127)
markScheme: 1 mark: 254
questions.explanation: Each iodine molecule contains two atoms: 2 × 127 = 254.

questions.question: Calculate the relative formula mass (Mr) of potassium iodide, KI. (Ar: K = 39, I = 127)
markScheme: 1 mark: 166
questions.explanation: KI contains one potassium and one iodine: 39 + 127 = 166.

questions.question: Chlorine boils at −34 °C and iodine boils at 184 °C. Estimate the boiling point of bromine, which lies between them, by calculating the mean of these two values.
markScheme: 1 mark: 75 °C
questions.explanation: 150 ÷ 2 = 75 °C. The real value is 59 °C, so the estimate is reasonable; it correctly predicts a liquid at room temperature.

questions.question:
0.71 g of chlorine reacts completely with excess potassium iodide solution.
Cl₂(aq) + 2KI(aq) → 2KCl(aq) + I₂(aq)
Calculate the mass of iodine produced. (Ar: Cl = 35.5, I = 127)
markScheme: 1 mark: moles Cl₂ = 0.71 ÷ 71 = 0.010 mol
1 mark: moles I₂ = 0.010 mol (1 : 1 ratio)
questions.explanation: Mr of Cl₂ is 71 and of I₂ is 254. The equation gives one mole of I₂ for every mole of Cl₂.

questions.question: Name the compound formed when chlorine reacts with potassium.
markScheme: 1 mark: potassium chloride
questions.explanation: Metal + halogen → metal halide. The halogen name changes from chlorine to chloride.

questions.question: State the colour of iodine in aqueous solution.
markScheme: 1 mark: brown (accept orange-brown or yellow-brown)
questions.explanation: Iodine solution is brown. Iodine vapour is purple and solid iodine is grey-black.

questions.question: Write a balanced symbol equation, with state symbols, for the reaction between chlorine and potassium bromide solution.
markScheme: 1 mark: correct formulae and balancing: Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂
1 mark: state symbols all (aq)
questions.explanation: Chlorine and bromine are diatomic, so 2KBr and 2KCl are needed to balance the equation.

questions.question: A student adds iodine solution to potassium bromide solution. Explain why no reaction takes place.
markScheme: 1 mark: iodine is less reactive than bromine (lower in Group 7)
1 mark: so it cannot displace bromine from its salt
questions.explanation: Only a more reactive halogen can displace a less reactive one.

questions.question: Explain why the halogens have similar chemical properties.
markScheme: 1 mark: they all have 7 electrons in the outer shell
1 mark: so they all react by gaining one electron (forming 1− ions) or sharing electrons
questions.explanation: Chemical properties depend on the outer shell, and all halogens have the same number of outer electrons.

questions.question: Sodium reacts with chlorine to form a white solid. Describe the type of compound formed and the ions it contains.
markScheme: 1 mark: an ionic compound / salt (sodium chloride)
1 mark: containing Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions
questions.explanation: Metal and non-metal combine by electron transfer: sodium loses one electron and chlorine gains one.

questions.question: Explain, in terms of electronic structure, why chlorine is more reactive than bromine.
markScheme: 1 mark: chlorine atoms have fewer shells, so the outer shell is closer to the nucleus
1 mark: there is less shielding, so there is a stronger attraction for an extra electron
1 mark: so chlorine gains an electron more easily
questions.explanation: The key idea is gaining an electron. Do not talk about losing electrons for halogens.

questions.question: Explain why iodine is a solid at room temperature but chlorine is a gas.
markScheme: 1 mark: iodine molecules are larger / have a higher relative molecular mass (254 v 71)
1 mark: so the forces between iodine molecules are stronger and need more energy to overcome (higher melting and boiling points)
questions.explanation: Melting and boiling separate molecules; the stronger intermolecular forces in iodine mean it melts at 114 °C.

questions.question: Bromine water is added to sodium iodide solution. Write the two half equations for this reaction and state which substance is reduced.
markScheme: 1 mark: Br₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Br⁻
1 mark: 2I⁻ → I₂ + 2e⁻
1 mark: bromine is reduced (it gains electrons)
questions.explanation: Bromine gains electrons (reduction); iodide ions lose electrons (oxidation). Sodium ions are spectators.

questions.question: Plan an experiment using displacement reactions to find the order of reactivity of chlorine, bromine and iodine. Describe the results you would expect and explain how they show the order of reactivity.
markScheme: Indicative content: use chlorine water, bromine water and iodine solution, and potassium chloride, potassium bromide and potassium iodide solutions; add a few drops of each halogen solution to a small volume of each halide solution in a spotting tile or test tubes; observe colour changes; do not test a halogen with its own halide; use the same volumes; expected results: chlorine water turns KBr orange and KI brown; bromine water turns KI brown but no change with KCl; iodine solution gives no change with KCl or KBr; a colour change shows a displacement has occurred; chlorine displaces both so it is most reactive; iodine displaces neither so it is least reactive; order Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂; safety: wear eye protection, work in a well-ventilated area because halogens are toxic.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a clear, workable method, correct expected results for all combinations, and a logical conclusion on the reactivity order.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a workable method with some correct results and a partial conclusion.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about mixing solutions, with few results or no clear conclusion.
questions.explanation: A table of results makes the order obvious: the halogen that causes the most colour changes is the most reactive.

Astatine is below iodine. Predict the state, colour and reactivity of astatine, and explain your predictions using the trends in the table and the electronic structure of the atoms.
markScheme: Indicative content: boiling point increases with Mr, so astatine has a boiling point above 184 °C and is a solid at room temperature; colour gets darker down the group, so astatine is very dark or black; reactivity decreases down the group, so astatine is the least reactive halogen; it has more shells, so its outer shell is further from the nucleus with more shielding; an electron is gained less easily; it will not displace iodine from iodide solutions.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): sensible predictions of state, colour and reactivity, each linked to a trend, with an electronic explanation of reactivity.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two predictions with little explanation.
questions.explanation: Use the trends explicitly: rising boiling point, darkening colour and decreasing reactivity.

questions.question:
Chlorine water is added to potassium bromide solution and the solution turns orange.
Explain this observation. Your answer should include a balanced symbol equation, the ionic equation, half equations, and an explanation in terms of electronic structure of why chlorine displaces bromine.
markScheme: Indicative content: chlorine is more reactive than bromine, so it displaces bromine; orange colour is due to bromine formed; Cl₂(aq) + 2KBr(aq) → 2KCl(aq) + Br₂(aq); ionic equation Cl₂(aq) + 2Br⁻(aq) → 2Cl⁻(aq) + Br₂(aq), K⁺ are spectator ions; half equations Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻ (reduction) and 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻ (oxidation); redox reaction; chlorine atoms are smaller, outer shell closer to the nucleus, less shielding, so stronger attraction for electrons; chlorine gains electrons more readily than bromine, so electrons are transferred from bromide ions to chlorine.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): all equations correct, oxidation and reduction correctly identified, and a clear electronic explanation of the relative reactivity.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): most equations correct with some identification of oxidation or reduction, and some explanation of reactivity.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): states that chlorine is more reactive and bromine is formed, with few correct equations.
questions.explanation: The halogen that attracts electrons more strongly takes them from the halide ion of the less reactive halogen.
